title: The Last Ferry
subtitle: Seven Days on Merriwick Island

listing.title: The Last Ferry ⛴️
listing.blurb: At 4:12 on a Thursday something lifts the bridges off Merriwick Island and sets them down in the park, and the things walking the avenues ignore anyone who keeps to their routine. You are a nurse, a line cook, a bus driver and three other ordinary people with seven days to find a way across the water. Levels 1–5.

synopsis: Merriwick is an island city of two million people: thirteen miles of granite between two rivers and a harbor, stacked with towers, threaded with subway, tied to the mainland by four bridges, two tunnels, a commuter railroad and a ferry that has run every thirty minutes for a century. At 4:12 on an ordinary October Thursday, the Visitors arrive. They do not land and they do not attack. The light changes, every phone on the island sounds the same tone, and the river spans of the Kingsgate and Concord Bridges lift into the air with the evening traffic still on them and are set down, intact and perfectly level, across the Greensward. A shimmer forms on the water a quarter of a mile offshore all the way round the island — survivors call it the Hem — and anything that crosses it is turned gently back. Fourteen-foot things on three legs walk the avenues, and they take anyone who runs, shouts or shoots, and they walk straight past the woman who keeps walking to the subway. The player characters are not soldiers. They are a retired transit cop, a bike messenger, an ER nurse, a line cook, a chemistry teacher and a tour-bus driver, and over seven days they will learn the one rule that matters — the Visitors do not see what the city does every day — and use it to scavenge, shelter, protect the people who attach themselves to them, and find a way off. There are several ways across the water and every one of them costs something. The Visitors are closing them one by one. And at 4:12 on the following Thursday, something is going to happen to everything still on the island; the last boat before it is the 3:45 from Pier Point.
hook: 4:12 P.M., Thursday, Union Terminal. The concourse is at the start of its evening rush: four hundred people under the great green-and-gold ceiling with its painted constellations, the departure board clattering, a busker on the east stair playing something by Bach on a saxophone. Then the light changes. Not dimmer — different, as if the sun had been swapped for a slightly more careful one. Every phone in the hall plays the same tone at once, a long low note none of them were built to make, and the departure board flips, all of it, to a row of blank white tiles. The busker stops. Into the silence comes a sound from outside like an enormous breath being drawn, and through the tall west windows, down the canyon of Forty-Second Street, four hundred people watch the river span of the Kingsgate Bridge rise out of the evening haze — whole, lit, with the rush-hour traffic still on it — turn once, slowly, like a hand being shown, and drift away north over the rooftops. Nobody screams for almost four seconds. Then everybody does.

setting.name: Merriwick Island
setting.description: Merriwick — 'the Wick' to the people who live there — is a fictional island city that feels like a great American harbor metropolis without being any real one, which means the GM owns the map. It is thirteen miles long and two wide, a spine of granite running north to south between the Westwater (a mile-wide tidal river to the west, with the mainland's cliffs and towns beyond) and the Tidewater (a swift, narrower strait to the east, with the borough of Ashford across it). At the south tip the island opens onto Lower Bay, a broad harbor with the mainland port of Calder Point three miles across it. At the north tip a narrow tidal creek called Devil's Kill separates the island's last wooded heights from the mainland. Before the Arrival, Merriwick was tied to everything else by the Kingsgate Bridge and the Sutter Street Bridge across the Tidewater, the Concord Bridge across the Kill at the north-east, the Harrow Bridge in the far north, the Holloway Tunnel under the Westwater, the two-track Northern Line commuter railroad across the Kill on a century-old swing bridge, the subway's Ashford Tubes under the Tidewater, and the Pier Point–Calder Point ferry, the Margaret Duane, every thirty minutes since 1924. Down the middle runs the Greensward, a park two and a half miles long, with a reservoir, a lawn, a tangle of woods and a zoo. South of it is the Meridian, the island's tall midtown, built around the cathedral-sized Union Terminal; below that the residential grid of the Middle Wards; and at the very bottom the Lower Ward, a narrow medieval tangle of financial towers ending at the Pier Point ferry terminal. North of the park are Harlow, dense and proud, and then the Steeps, a hill-country of old forts, apartment blocks on cliffs and the last woods on the island. Under all of it runs the Under: nine subway lines, a hundred and forty stations, and a great many tunnels nobody has walked in decades.
setting.atmosphere: Ordinary life under an extraordinary sky. The horror here is not gore and it is not war: it is a perfectly normal city continuing around you in a way it should not. Traffic lights still change, on their timers, for streets with no cars. The Set — people the Visitors have taken — stand on corners and in lobbies doing the last thing they were doing, gently, over and over: a man hailing a cab that will never come, a choir in a church basement singing the same four bars. The Visitors are vast, patient and beautiful, and they are not angry; they do not even appear to notice anyone who is doing what Merriwick does every day. The dread is attention. Every sound you make is a question you are asking the sky. The tone is grounded and human and specific — the smell of a deli at 6 A.M., the weight of a ten-year-old on your back, the exact number of rounds in a borrowed revolver — and the campaign should feel like the first night of a blackout that does not end. There are moments of terrible beauty. There is very little fighting, and almost none of it is against the Visitors. Nobody in this campaign is a hero yet; by the end, some of them will be.

regions.name: The Meridian and Union Terminal
regions.description: Midtown: forty-storey canyons, the Hallam Tower at 1,410 feet, theatres, hotels, department stores and the vast vaulted concourse of Union Terminal, from which nine subway lines and two commuter railroads radiate. The campaign begins here. On Day 1 the Meridian is a stampede; by Day 3 it is a ghost town of perfectly working traffic lights, Set office workers riding escalators in the lobbies, and survivors in libraries, churches and hotel basements. The Merriwick Public Library on Forty-First Street, guarded by two stone owls, becomes the party's first shelter.

regions.name: The Greensward
regions.description: The island's great park: two and a half miles of lawns, woods, ponds and stone bridges, with the Reservoir at its heart and the Merriwick Museum of Natural History on its western edge. On Day 1 the Visitors set the river spans of the Kingsgate and Concord Bridges down across the Great Lawn, level and intact, with the cars still on them, and a Lantern — a vast, slow, luminous column of something alive — settles into the Reservoir. The Set are brought here: by Day 3 there are thousands of them standing in the Greensward in loose rows, each one quietly living the moment they were taken.

regions.name: Lower Ward and Pier Point
regions.description: The narrow, ancient southern tip of the island: the Exchange, the old customs house, crooked streets laid out on cow paths, towers so close together that the sky is a slot. At the bottom, Pier Point: a waterfront park, an old stone fort, the Harbor Acoustic Monitoring station and the Pier Point Ferry Terminal, where the Margaret Duane still runs her timetable with her Set crew aboard. A second Lantern stands in Lower Bay a mile off the Point, taller than any building on the island, lit from inside like a paper lamp.

regions.name: The West Side and the Holloway Tunnel
regions.description: The long Westwater waterfront: piers, a highway, warehouses converted to lofts, and the great tiled portal of the Holloway Tunnel, a mile and six-tenths under the river to the mainland. At 4:12 the tunnel was full of rush-hour traffic, and much of it is still in there. Lt. Dana Castellane of the Merriwick Police Department's Emergency Service Unit holds the tunnel's ventilation building as a shelter for four hundred people and has a plan for the jam.

regions.name: Harlow, the Steeps and Devil's Kill
regions.description: North of the park: Harlow's brownstones, churches and avenues, then the Steeps — cliffs, old revolutionary forts, apartment blocks on stilts of granite, the last woods on the island — and at the very top the Devil's Kill, a hundred yards of fast tidal creek between the island and the mainland. The Concord and Harrow Bridges are gone. The Northern Line commuter railroad still crosses the Kill on its 1907 swing bridge, which stood open for barge traffic at 4:12 and is open still. The Ushers den in the Steeps' woods, and they are fast.

regions.name: The Under
regions.description: The subway: a hundred and forty stations and their tunnels, ventilation shafts and abandoned platforms, the Ashford Tubes under the Tidewater, and a deep freight tunnel from the Meridian down to the Lower Ward that has not carried anything since 1961. The power went on Day 2. The Visitors do not go below ground, but the Glitter drifts down stairways like dust, and the Under is very dark, very quiet, and full of people who went down there on Day 1 and have not come up.

campaignRules.name: Ordinary People
campaignRules.description: The player characters are civilians. Their class is an aptitude, not a job: the Soldier is a retired transit cop, the Brawler a line cook, the Face a tour-bus driver. Merriwick has strict gun laws and almost nobody carries; firearms and ammunition are rare, precious and loud, and finding ammunition while scavenging is DC 20. Characters without the relevant proficiency group fire guns with no proficiency bonus. Expect the party to reach the Last Ferry with a handful of guns and a few dozen rounds between them, and to have been right not to use most of them.

campaignRules.name: In Pattern
campaignRules.description: THE CORE RULE OF THE CAMPAIGN. The Visitors perceive Merriwick as a pattern — the enormous, repeating shape of what the city does every day — and they do not perceive anything that is part of it. A person walking at an ordinary pace along a street, a commuter going down into the subway, a deli opening at six, a car driving in lane at the speed limit with its lights on, a ferry running its timetable: these are In Pattern, and Stilts and Ushers will walk straight past them, even within arm's reach, unless the Attention in the scene is already at 6. Out of Pattern is anything the city does not do every day: running, shouting, screaming, gunfire, explosions, car alarms, breaking glass, climbing a building, a crowd panicking, a child crying in the street. Holding pattern under stress — walking past a Stilt at a normal pace while it bends over you — is a Keep Walking check: WIS (Insight) or CHA (Performance), DC 10 for something ordinary, DC 13 with a Visitor within 30 ft, DC 15 within 10 ft or while carrying or leading someone who is struggling. Failure means you flinch, stop or run: you are Out of Pattern for one round and the Attention rises by 1. Players will discover this rule; do not state it. June Halvorsen notices it about forty minutes after the Arrival in lf-scenario-001, and Yusuf Haddad proves it in lf-scenario-002.

campaignRules.name: Attention
campaignRules.description: Every scene in the open has an Attention clock from 0 to 6, tracked by the GM and shown to the players as a mood (0 still, 2 the Glitter drifts, 4 something is walking this way, 6 the sky is looking at you). Add: running or shouting +1 per round; a scream, a child crying, breaking glass, an engine starting or headlights at night outside traffic hours +1; a car alarm or fire alarm +2; unsuppressed gunfire +3 the first shot in a scene and +1 per later exchange (suppressed: +1 the first time); an explosion +4; killing a Stilt goes straight to 6 and spreads Attention 4 to every adjacent district. Remove 1 for every ten minutes of complete pattern-quiet, and 2 if a Lullaby is playing. Thresholds: at 2, a Glitter swarm drifts into the scene and records; at 4, a Stilt walks in to read the place (it will Lift whatever is Out of Pattern); at 6, a Stilt and 1d4 Ushers arrive and herd, and anything Out of Pattern will be taken to the nearest Lantern. Indoors, the Attention is a building's, not a street's: noise travels through a building completely and through a block barely. Underground, Attention rises at half rate, and the Visitors do not come down — but what they hear at a stairhead, they wait at.

campaignRules.name: Alien Dread
campaignRules.description: The first time in a scene a character sees a Stilt or an Usher at close range (within 60 ft), or sees someone Lifted, they make a WIS save DC 12; within 300 ft of a Lantern, DC 15. On a failure the character is Shaken (disadvantage on WIS and CHA checks and saves until a short rest) — which matters, because Keep Walking checks are WIS and CHA. A character who is already Shaken and fails again is frightened of the source for 1 minute, and a frightened character who cannot see a way to retreat must succeed on a Keep Walking check every round or run. A Face's Rally ends frightened. A character who succeeds on a Dread save against a given Visitor type is immune to Dread from that type until the next dawn. By lf-scenario-004 the party should be immune to most things except the Harbor Lantern.

campaignRules.name: The Lullaby
campaignRules.description: Discovered by Yusuf Haddad in lf-scenario-002. A looping recording of an ordinary Merriwick place — a concourse, a deli, a subway platform — played from a speaker reads to the Visitors as pattern, and anything within 30 ft of it is partly hidden: Attention gains in that radius are reduced by 1 (to a minimum of 0) and Keep Walking checks are made with advantage. The recording must be of the place it is played in, or of somewhere very like it (a deli sounds wrong in a church). A Lullaby needs a speaker and power; phones die; Bluetooth speakers last about 6 hours. Any Tech or Scientist can make a new one with a recorder and ten minutes (no check), but it only works for a scene once the Glitter has recorded it twice — after that, the Visitors have heard that loop and it becomes novel. Make the players keep recording new ones.

campaignRules.name: Scavenging
campaignRules.description: A scavenge is a 30-minute search of one building, made by one character with help from others: Investigation (shops, offices, apartments), Streetwise (knowing where things will be), Survival (parks and waterfront) or Mechanics (garages, utility rooms). DC 10: food and water for the party for a day, batteries, flashlights, basic first aid (a medkit's worth on a 15+). DC 15: medicine (antibiotics, insulin, painkillers), a working radio, a portable power bank or generator fuel, tools, bolt cutters, a bicycle, a cart. DC 20: a firearm (a .38 revolver, a 9mm pistol or a shotgun, with 1d6+4 rounds), a car with keys and fuel, a hospital trauma kit, a marine VHF radio. Each building can be scavenged once. Scavenging is noisy work: unless the character takes ten minutes more and makes the check at disadvantage, it adds +1 Attention when it ends. Power fails island-wide at noon on Day 2; phone networks fail on Day 1 evening except for the occasional text; by Day 5 food in the Meridian is scarce (DC +2).

campaignRules.name: Civilians
campaignRules.description: Frightened people attach themselves to anyone who seems to know what they are doing, and the party will collect them: Benny's fourteen tourists, June's three students, the forty-one people in the Library, nine ventilated patients, a city. The GM tracks civilians as Groups (up to about 20 people each) with a Calm score from 0 to 5. A Group at Calm 3+ can Keep Walking as one person, using the best Persuasion or Performance of the character leading it. At Calm 1–2 it rolls with disadvantage. At Calm 0 it panics: it is Out of Pattern, adds +1 Attention per round, and scatters. Calm drops by 1 for a Lifting seen, a gunshot, a night without food or sleep, or a member Lifted; it rises by 1 for a meal, a night's sleep somewhere safe, a successful Rally or a DC 13 Persuasion from someone they trust. Keep a running tally of every civilian the party gets across the water — the campaign's epilogue is built from it, name by name where you can. The Visitors do not hurt the Set and do not kill on purpose; the cost of failing civilians is that they stay on the island at 4:12 on the final Thursday (Day 8).

campaignRules.name: The Set
campaignRules.description: People the Visitors Lift are carried to a Lantern and returned, within the hour, to the Greensward (or to a Lantern's foot), Set: standing, sitting or walking a few steps, gently living the moment they were taken, over and over. A Set person is warm, breathing and unharmed, does not eat, does not tire, and cannot be moved more than a few feet before they drift back. They can be woken: someone who knows them must say their name and something true that the Set person has never heard before (a confession, a piece of news, a secret) — a CHA (Persuasion) check DC 15, made with advantage by family or a lover. A woken person drops to the ground, is Shaken for a day, and for the next hour counts as Out of Pattern in everything they do. Most of the woken want to go back; the Set are not suffering, and some will say it is the best moment of their life. Nobody is killed by being Set. What happens to the Set at 4:12 on the final Thursday is the campaign's last revelation.

campaignRules.name: The Hem and the Countdown
campaignRules.description: The Hem is a faint shimmer on the water about a quarter of a mile off every shore, and on the Kill a line down the middle of the creek. Anything Out of Pattern that crosses it — a swimmer, a stolen speedboat, a helicopter, a bridge-jumper — is turned back: slowed, turned, and set down on the island shore, usually Set. Anything crossing that is In Pattern passes, for as long as the Visitors leave that route open: the ferry on her timetable, the Northern Line trains at their scheduled times, traffic in the Holloway Tunnel. The Visitors are closing routes from the largest to the smallest. Day 1: the Kingsgate, Concord and Harrow Bridges and the subway's Ashford Tubes. Day 4: the Sutter Street Bridge, which has stood jammed solid with Day 1 traffic all week (pedestrians who tried to walk across it were turned back Set), is lifted in the morning in front of half the East Side. Dawn of Day 6 (Tuesday): the Holloway Tunnel (the Glitter fills it solid). Midnight at the end of Day 7 (Wednesday): the Northern Line. 4:12 P.M. on Day 8 — Thursday, one week to the second after the Arrival: everything. Each route the survivors use, the Visitors notice and close early (see lf-scenario-003). Days are counted from the Arrival: Day 1 Thursday, Day 2 Friday, Day 3 Saturday, Day 4 Sunday, Day 5 Monday, Day 6 Tuesday, Day 7 Wednesday, Day 8 Thursday. Every clock on the island has been drifting slightly — wristwatches, church bells, the Union Terminal clock — and by dawn on Day 6 they all agree, to the second, with each other and with nothing outside. The last boat before 4:12 on Day 8 is the 3:45 from Pier Point.

campaignRules.name: Ammunition and Gunplay
campaignRules.description: Use the core gunplay rules in full. Deduct rounds with TrackResources 'use' once per exchange, never in bulk afterwards; out of ammo means out. Remember the Noise rule from the core rules applies doubly here: every unsuppressed shot is +3 Attention in the scene. Stilts and Ushers have no conventional anatomy: called shots do not work on them.

explorationRules: This is a seven-day campaign on one island, and the clock is the campaign. Track days and hours openly: the players should always know what day it is and roughly what time, because the pattern depends on time (a street at 8 A.M. is full of commuters' ghosts and can be walked; the same street at 2 A.M. cannot). Merriwick is thirteen miles long: walking in pattern covers about a mile in twenty minutes; Calla's roof and Under routes double that and cost a climb or a dark tunnel; a vehicle in pattern does a mile in three minutes if the street is clear and is a rolling Attention problem if it is not. The power fails at noon on Day 2 and the night after that is very dark, very quiet and very dangerous. Run the city as a place that is still trying to be itself: traffic signals changing for nobody, an automatic sprinkler on a lawn in the Greensward, a Set doorman holding a door, a radio in a bodega still tuned to a mainland station playing the news about you. Let the players find things out by watching — the Visitors are consistent, and a party that observes before it acts should be rewarded every time. The Visitors do not fight; they read, they record, and they Lift. Most of the campaign's violence is human: looters, frightened armed people, Castellane's explosives, and the occasional Usher pressed into a corner. Combat against a Stilt is possible and nearly always a mistake, and the GM should let it be both. Between scenes, improvise survival: a meal cooked on a camp stove in a library, a child who will not stop humming, a rooftop at night where the Lanterns look like paper lamps, a Set man in a phone booth who has been about to say 'I love you' for four days. Every scenario offers more than one route; none of them is free. The goal of the campaign is the far shore, and the measure of it is how many people the party brings with them.
